rv.q: This is tough, unflinching drama staged and performed by people with a fierce emotional investment in telling this story and keeping this painful history alive for generations inclined to forget.

Your eyes are pretty much guaranteed to start stinging before the first act is over, and by the play’s end even people who think they have no patience for polemical theater may find their resistance has melted into tears.

"The Normal Heart" was never meant to be a subtle work. Larry Kramer wrote it in 1985 to be a shock to the system, an alarm siren, a blunt instrument to bludgeon Ed Koch’s New York, Ronald Reagan’s Washington, the indifferent press and complacent medical industry into acknowledging the mysterious disease destroying gay men.

Larry Kramer's furious 1985 drama about the early years of the AIDS crisis burns with undiminished urgency in this superb Broadway revival, directed with searing intensity by Joel Grey and George C. Wolfe.

It’s true that "The Normal Heart," Larry Kramer’s fiery 1985 docu-like drama about the AIDS pandemic, suffers from agit-prop agita, even in this first-rate production starring Joe Mantello and Ellen Barkin and co-helmed with enormous heart by Joel Grey and George C. Wolfe.
Joe Mantello's production of Larry Kramer's AIDS-era drama is a powerhouse revival that crackles with righteous anger and deep humanity.

But as a chronicle of a historical moment, The Normal Heart still packs a serious emotional wallop.

A semi-fictionalized account of the beginning of the AIDS crisis and the efforts of a group of dedicated activists to spur the city and country into action, this work, first seen in 1985 in a landmark production at the Public Theater, is relentlessly gripping and moving.

cn.t: Kramer's searing 1985 AIDS drama remains a powerful, urgent piece of political theater in this passionately acted Broadway revival, though some find its agitprop approach heavy-handed. The stellar cast delivers emotionally devastating performances.
